edges.effect_quant: Cooking-class interventions generally improve food agency, cooking confidence, and selected diet-quality measures, but changes in dietary intake are often modest. In one adult weight-loss trial, both hands-on and demonstration cooking arms improved Healthy Eating Index scores, while child and student cooking programs tended to improve healthy-eating behaviors or food quality indicators more than they changed hard clinical outcomes.
edges.population: children, students, or adults participating in structured cooking-skill or culinary classes
edges.mechanism: Cooking classes can improve diet quality by increasing confidence, food-preparation skills, and willingness to prepare healthier foods at home. They may also reduce reliance on ultra-processed convenience meals by lowering the practical barriers to home cooking.
edges.summary: The evidence suggests cooking classes can support healthier eating patterns, especially through better cooking confidence and food choices, but the effect on measured diet quality is usually modest rather than transformative. Benefits are more consistent when classes are hands-on and repeated over several sessions.
edges.caveats: The cooking-intervention literature is heterogeneous and often small, with variable measures of diet quality and follow-up. Some studies show strong gains in cooking self-efficacy but only limited or short-lived changes in actual dietary intake.
